We focus on the one-shot ultimatum game for three main reasons. First, it eliminates history-dependent learning and reputation effects, leaving a unique subgame-perfect equilibrium that provides a clean theoretical benchmark. Second, recent cross-task evaluations by Mei et al. (2024), who compared large-language-model agents with human subjects on several classic economic games, including the ultimatum game, show that the one-shot ultimatum game exhibits the largest human-AI performance gap. This makes the one-shot ultimatum game a stringent test bed: if generative agents can narrow that gap here, the implication for other interaction settings is even stronger. Third, a single-round design keeps prompts concise and prevents chain-ofthought content from leaking across rounds, which could otherwise induce artificial correlations in multi-round simulations. Taken together, these considerations make the one-shot ultimatum game the most interpretable and demanding environment for assessing whether enhanced reasoning enables LLM agents to approximate human bargaining behavior

Generative AI refers to a class of models that autonomously produce new, plausible data samples across various modalities—from text and images to audio and beyond. Unlike discriminative models that classify or predict within existing data boundaries, generative models learn the underlying data distribution itself, enabling them to synthesize entirely new outputs (Goodfellow et al. 2020; Ramesh et al. 2022). This paradigm shift—from recognition to generation—has created models that are not just analytical but creative, capable of mimicking the structure of real-world behavior and expression. In this sense, generative AI offers more than technological novelty; it marks a methodological transformation in how we model social phenomena

From a behavioral modeling standpoint, gpt-4 can be interpreted as a statistical knowledge base constructed from human language and interaction patterns. Its training corpus contains linguistic patterns that reflect social norms, strategic heuristics, and communicative conventions across cultural contexts (Lorè and Heydari 2024). This enables the model to produce responses that are not only linguistically fluent but also behaviorally plausible, a property that has led to its adoption in simulating agents for bargaining, negotiation, and multi-agent coordination (Dell’Acqua et al. 2023; Phelps and Russell 2024; Park et al. 2023). Crucially, this generative capacity enables LLMs to function as foundation models—general-purpose substrates that can be adapted to various downstream tasks without the need for retraining

Nevertheless, several limitations must be addressed when deploying LLMs as behavioral agents. First, hallucinations, plausible but incorrect outputs, can emerge, especially under poorly constrained prompts (Bubeck et al. 2023). These are a byproduct of the model’s reliance on learned statistical associations rather than grounded world models. Second, LLMs inherit biases from their training data, which can affect their decision-making in subtle but impactful ways (e.g., favoring certain persuasion styles, exhibiting implicit demographic stereotypes) (Blodgett et al. 2020; Caliskan et al. 2017). Third, these models remain black boxes in terms of interpretability: while their outputs are analyzable, their internal reasoning processes are not directly accessible

We therefore adopt two prompting strategies—(i) few-shot prompting, where the model is shown a small number of annotated examples to guide output style and logic (Brown et al. 2020), and (ii) chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, which explicitly instructs the model to articulate intermediate reasoning steps (Wei et al. 2022)—not as general mitigation techniques, but as scaffolding methods to influence the reasoning quality of agent decisions in structured tasks. These strategies have been shown to enhance coherence, inference depth, and contextual relevance in complex queries

The simulation strategy involved generating 1000 independent decisions for each unique combination of role (proposer/responder), prompt type, and temperature. While this number is not derived from a formal power analysis, it was selected based on two main considerations. First, prior work Kitadai et al. (2023) employed the same sample size and demonstrated that it was sufficient to reveal stable and interpretable distributions of agent behavior. Second, to assess the robustness of our findings, we also tested larger sets of examples (15 and 20 samples) to explore the presence or absence of significant differences in the simulation outcomes. Additionally, we investigate the stability of our results by repeating the selection of 10 examples with different random seeds. Through these robustness check, we confirmed the consistency of results across samples of this size (see Sect. 4). Moreover, the use of chain-of-thought prompting with large models incurs substantial computational cost per generation, making higher sample sizes impractical. Thus, 1000 strikes a balance between statistical resolution and feasibility in simulation-based research

Our findings indicate that LLMs, even when endowed with advanced reasoning capabilities, do not naturally exhibit human-like economic behavior unless explicitly guided by prompts that incorporate social context. Consequently, using LLMdriven MAS as stand-ins for real human groups is currently unwarranted. Moreover, as LLMs continue to improve, there is a risk that such systems could misleadingly portray human behavior as excessively rational. Thus, treating LLMs as direct substitutes for human subjects is a flawed approach. This does not preclude the possibility of employing LLMs in economic modeling or behavioral simulation, but doing so effectively will require deliberate methodological scaffolding. If one seeks to explore such potential within the framework of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis by Huh et al. (2024), careful design and contextualization become essential
